# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/regex/1.12.4/src/regex/lib.rs.html

# regex/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)/*!
[2](https://docs.rs#2)This crate provides routines for searching strings for matches of a [regular
[3](https://docs.rs#3)expression] (aka "regex"). The regex syntax supported by this crate is similar
[4](https://docs.rs#4)to other regex engines, but it lacks several features that are not known how to
[5](https://docs.rs#5)implement efficiently. This includes, but is not limited to, look-around and
[6](https://docs.rs#6)backreferences. In exchange, all regex searches in this crate have worst case
[7](https://docs.rs#7)`O(m * n)` time complexity, where `m` is proportional to the size of the regex
[8](https://docs.rs#8)and `n` is proportional to the size of the string being searched.
[9](https://docs.rs#9)
[10](https://docs.rs#10)[regular expression]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_expression
[11](https://docs.rs#11)
[12](https://docs.rs#12)If you just want API documentation, then skip to the [`Regex`] type. Otherwise,
[13](https://docs.rs#13)here's a quick example showing one way of parsing the output of a grep-like
[14](https://docs.rs#14)program:
[15](https://docs.rs#15)
[16](https://docs.rs#16)```rust
[17](https://docs.rs#17)use regex::Regex;
[18](https://docs.rs#18)
[19](https://docs.rs#19)let re = Regex::new(r"(?m)^([^:]+):([0-9]+):(.+)$").unwrap();
[20](https://docs.rs#20)let hay = "\
[21](https://docs.rs#21)path/to/foo:54:Blue Harvest
[22](https://docs.rs#22)path/to/bar:90:Something, Something, Something, Dark Side
[23](https://docs.rs#23)path/to/baz:3:It's a Trap!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)";
[25](https://docs.rs#25)
[26](https://docs.rs#26)let mut results = vec![];
[27](https://docs.rs#27)for (_, [path, lineno, line]) in re.captures_iter(hay).map(|c| c.extract()) {
[28](https://docs.rs#28)    results.push((path, lineno.parse::<u64>()?, line));
[29](https://docs.rs#29)}
[30](https://docs.rs#30)assert_eq!(results, vec![
[31](https://docs.rs#31)    ("path/to/foo", 54, "Blue Harvest"),
[32](https://docs.rs#32)    ("path/to/bar", 90, "Something, Something, Something, Dark Side"),
[33](https://docs.rs#33)    ("path/to/baz", 3, "It's a Trap!"),
[34](https://docs.rs#34)]);
[35](https://docs.rs#35)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[36](https://docs.rs#36)```
[37](https://docs.rs#37)
[38](https://docs.rs#38)# Overview
[39](https://docs.rs#39)
[40](https://docs.rs#40)The primary type in this crate is a [`Regex`]. Its most important methods are
[41](https://docs.rs#41)as follows:
[42](https://docs.rs#42)
[43](https://docs.rs#43)* [`Regex::new`] compiles a regex using the default configuration. A
[44](https://docs.rs#44)[`RegexBuilder`] permits setting a non-default configuration. (For example,
[45](https://docs.rs#45)case insensitive matching, verbose mode and others.)
[46](https://docs.rs#46)* [`Regex::is_match`] reports whether a match exists in a particular haystack.
[47](https://docs.rs#47)* [`Regex::find`] reports the byte offsets of a match in a haystack, if one
[48](https://docs.rs#48)exists. [`Regex::find_iter`] returns an iterator over all such matches.
[49](https://docs.rs#49)* [`Regex::captures`] returns a [`Captures`], which reports both the byte
[50](https://docs.rs#50)offsets of a match in a haystack and the byte offsets of each matching capture
[51](https://docs.rs#51)group from the regex in the haystack.
[52](https://docs.rs#52)[`Regex::captures_iter`] returns an iterator over all such matches.
[53](https://docs.rs#53)
[54](https://docs.rs#54)There is also a [`RegexSet`], which permits searching for multiple regex
[55](https://docs.rs#55)patterns simultaneously in a single search. However, it currently only reports
[56](https://docs.rs#56)which patterns match and *not* the byte offsets of a match.
[57](https://docs.rs#57)
[58](https://docs.rs#58)Otherwise, this top-level crate documentation is organized as follows:
[59](https://docs.rs#59)
[60](https://docs.rs#60)* [Usage](#usage) shows how to add the `regex` crate to your Rust project.
[61](https://docs.rs#61)* [Examples](#examples) provides a limited selection of regex search examples.
[62](https://docs.rs#62)* [Performance](#performance) provides a brief summary of how to optimize regex
[63](https://docs.rs#63)searching speed.
[64](https://docs.rs#64)* [Unicode](#unicode) discusses support for non-ASCII patterns.
[65](https://docs.rs#65)* [Syntax](#syntax) enumerates the specific regex syntax supported by this
[66](https://docs.rs#66)crate.
[67](https://docs.rs#67)* [Untrusted input](#untrusted-input) discusses how this crate deals with regex
[68](https://docs.rs#68)patterns or haystacks that are untrusted.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)* [Crate features](#crate-features) documents the Cargo features that can be
[70](https://docs.rs#70)enabled or disabled for this crate.
[71](https://docs.rs#71)* [Other crates](#other-crates) links to other crates in the `regex` family.
[72](https://docs.rs#72)
[73](https://docs.rs#73)# Usage
[74](https://docs.rs#74)
[75](https://docs.rs#75)The `regex` crate is [on crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/regex) and can be
[76](https://docs.rs#76)used by adding `regex` to your dependencies in your project's `Cargo.toml`.
[77](https://docs.rs#77)Or more simply, just run `cargo add regex`.
[78](https://docs.rs#78)
[79](https://docs.rs#79)Here is a complete example that creates a new Rust project, adds a dependency
[80](https://docs.rs#80)on `regex`, creates the source code for a regex search and then runs the
[81](https://docs.rs#81)program.
[82](https://docs.rs#82)
[83](https://docs.rs#83)First, create the project in a new directory:
[84](https://docs.rs#84)
[85](https://docs.rs#85)```text
[86](https://docs.rs#86)$ mkdir regex-example
[87](https://docs.rs#87)$ cd regex-example
[88](https://docs.rs#88)$ cargo init
[89](https://docs.rs#89)```
[90](https://docs.rs#90)
[91](https://docs.rs#91)Second, add a dependency on `regex`:
[92](https://docs.rs#92)
[93](https://docs.rs#93)```text
[94](https://docs.rs#94)$ cargo add regex
[95](https://docs.rs#95)```
[96](https://docs.rs#96)
[97](https://docs.rs#97)Third, edit `src/main.rs`. Delete what's there and replace it with this:
[98](https://docs.rs#98)
[99](https://docs.rs#99)```
[100](https://docs.rs#100)use regex::Regex;
[101](https://docs.rs#101)
[102](https://docs.rs#102)fn main() {
[103](https://docs.rs#103)    let re = Regex::new(r"Hello (?<name>\w+)!").unwrap();
[104](https://docs.rs#104)    let Some(caps) = re.captures("Hello Murphy!") else {
[105](https://docs.rs#105)        println!("no match!");
[106](https://docs.rs#106)        return;
[107](https://docs.rs#107)    };
[108](https://docs.rs#108)    println!("The name is: {}", &caps["name"]);
[109](https://docs.rs#109)}
[110](https://docs.rs#110)```
[111](https://docs.rs#111)
[112](https://docs.rs#112)Fourth, run it with `cargo run`:
[113](https://docs.rs#113)
[114](https://docs.rs#114)```text
[115](https://docs.rs#115)$ cargo run
[116](https://docs.rs#116)   Compiling memchr v2.5.0
[117](https://docs.rs#117)   Compiling regex-syntax v0.7.1
[118](https://docs.rs#118)   Compiling aho-corasick v1.0.1
[119](https://docs.rs#119)   Compiling regex v1.8.1
[120](https://docs.rs#120)   Compiling regex-example v0.1.0 (/tmp/regex-example)
[121](https://docs.rs#121)    Finished dev [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 4.22s
[122](https://docs.rs#122)     Running `target/debug/regex-example`
[123](https://docs.rs#123)The name is: Murphy
[124](https://docs.rs#124)```
[125](https://docs.rs#125)
[126](https://docs.rs#126)The first time you run the program will show more output like above. But
[127](https://docs.rs#127)subsequent runs shouldn't have to re-compile the dependencies.
[128](https://docs.rs#128)
[129](https://docs.rs#129)# Examples
[130](https://docs.rs#130)
[131](https://docs.rs#131)This section provides a few examples, in tutorial style, showing how to
[132](https://docs.rs#132)search a haystack with a regex. There are more examples throughout the API
[133](https://docs.rs#133)documentation.
[134](https://docs.rs#134)
[135](https://docs.rs#135)Before starting though, it's worth defining a few terms:
[136](https://docs.rs#136)
[137](https://docs.rs#137)* A **regex** is a Rust value whose type is `Regex`. We use `re` as a
[138](https://docs.rs#138)variable name for a regex.
[139](https://docs.rs#139)* A **pattern** is the string that is used to build a regex. We use `pat` as
[140](https://docs.rs#140)a variable name for a pattern.
[141](https://docs.rs#141)* A **haystack** is the string that is searched by a regex. We use `hay` as a
[142](https://docs.rs#142)variable name for a haystack.
[143](https://docs.rs#143)
[144](https://docs.rs#144)Sometimes the words "regex" and "pattern" are used interchangeably.
[145](https://docs.rs#145)
[146](https://docs.rs#146)General use of regular expressions in this crate proceeds by compiling a
[147](https://docs.rs#147)**pattern** into a **regex**, and then using that regex to search, split or
[148](https://docs.rs#148)replace parts of a **haystack**.
[149](https://docs.rs#149)
[150](https://docs.rs#150)### Example: find a middle initial
[151](https://docs.rs#151)
[152](https://docs.rs#152)We'll start off with a very simple example: a regex that looks for a specific
[153](https://docs.rs#153)name but uses a wildcard to match a middle initial. Our pattern serves as
[154](https://docs.rs#154)something like a template that will match a particular name with *any* middle
[155](https://docs.rs#155)initial.
[156](https://docs.rs#156)
[157](https://docs.rs#157)```rust
[158](https://docs.rs#158)use regex::Regex;
[159](https://docs.rs#159)
[160](https://docs.rs#160)// We use 'unwrap()' here because it would be a bug in our program if the
[161](https://docs.rs#161)// pattern failed to compile to a regex. Panicking in the presence of a bug
[162](https://docs.rs#162)// is okay.
[163](https://docs.rs#163)let re = Regex::new(r"Homer (.)\. Simpson").unwrap();
[164](https://docs.rs#164)let hay = "Homer J. Simpson";
[165](https://docs.rs#165)let Some(caps) = re.captures(hay) else { return };
[166](https://docs.rs#166)assert_eq!("J", &caps[1]);
[167](https://docs.rs#167)```
[168](https://docs.rs#168)
[169](https://docs.rs#169)There are a few things worth noticing here in our first example:
[170](https://docs.rs#170)
[171](https://docs.rs#171)* The `.` is a special pattern meta character that means "match any single
[172](https://docs.rs#172)character except for new lines." (More precisely, in this crate, it means
[173](https://docs.rs#173)"match any UTF-8 encoding of any Unicode scalar value other than `\n`.")
[174](https://docs.rs#174)* We can match an actual `.` literally by escaping it, i.e., `\.`.
[175](https://docs.rs#175)* We use Rust's [raw strings] to avoid needing to deal with escape sequences in
[176](https://docs.rs#176)both the regex pattern syntax and in Rust's string literal syntax. If we didn't
[177](https://docs.rs#177)use raw strings here, we would have had to use `\\.` to match a literal `.`
[178](https://docs.rs#178)character. That is, `r"\."` and `"\\."` are equivalent patterns.
[179](https://docs.rs#179)* We put our wildcard `.` instruction in parentheses. These parentheses have a
[180](https://docs.rs#180)special meaning that says, "make whatever part of the haystack matches within
[181](https://docs.rs#181)these parentheses available as a capturing group." After finding a match, we
[182](https://docs.rs#182)access this capture group with `&caps[1]`.
[183](https://docs.rs#183)
[184](https://docs.rs#184)[raw strings]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/reference/tokens.html#raw-string-literals
[185](https://docs.rs#185)
[186](https://docs.rs#186)Otherwise, we execute a search using `re.captures(hay)` and return from our
[187](https://docs.rs#187)function if no match occurred. We then reference the middle initial by asking
[188](https://docs.rs#188)for the part of the haystack that matched the capture group indexed at `1`.
[189](https://docs.rs#189)(The capture group at index 0 is implicit and always corresponds to the entire
[190](https://docs.rs#190)match. In this case, that's `Homer J. Simpson`.)
[191](https://docs.rs#191)
[192](https://docs.rs#192)### Example: named capture groups
[193](https://docs.rs#193)
[194](https://docs.rs#194)Continuing from our middle initial example above, we can tweak the pattern
[195](https://docs.rs#195)slightly to give a name to the group that matches the middle initial:
[196](https://docs.rs#196)
[197](https://docs.rs#197)```rust
[198](https://docs.rs#198)use regex::Regex;
[199](https://docs.rs#199)
[200](https://docs.rs#200)// Note that (?P<middle>.) is a different way to spell the same thing.
[201](https://docs.rs#201)let re = Regex::new(r"Homer (?<middle>.)\. Simpson").unwrap();
[202](https://docs.rs#202)let hay = "Homer J. Simpson";
[203](https://docs.rs#203)let Some(caps) = re.captures(hay) else { return };
[204](https://docs.rs#204)assert_eq!("J", &caps["middle"]);
[205](https://docs.rs#205)```
[206](https://docs.rs#206)
[207](https://docs.rs#207)Giving a name to a group can be useful when there are multiple groups in
[208](https://docs.rs#208)a pattern. It makes the code referring to those groups a bit easier to
[209](https://docs.rs#209)understand.
[210](https://docs.rs#210)
[211](https://docs.rs#211)### Example: validating a particular date format
[212](https://docs.rs#212)
[213](https://docs.rs#213)This examples shows how to confirm whether a haystack, in its entirety, matches
[214](https://docs.rs#214)a particular date format:
[215](https://docs.rs#215)
[216](https://docs.rs#216)```rust
[217](https://docs.rs#217)use regex::Regex;
[218](https://docs.rs#218)
[219](https://docs.rs#219)let re = Regex::new(r"^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$").unwrap();
[220](https://docs.rs#220)assert!(re.is_match("2010-03-14"));
[221](https://docs.rs#221)```
[222](https://docs.rs#222)
[223](https://docs.rs#223)Notice the use of the `^` and `$` anchors. In this crate, every regex search is
[224](https://docs.rs#224)run with an implicit `(?s:.)*?` at the beginning of its pattern, which allows
[225](https://docs.rs#225)the regex to match anywhere in a haystack. Anchors, as above, can be used to
[226](https://docs.rs#226)ensure that the full haystack matches a pattern.
[227](https://docs.rs#227)
[228](https://docs.rs#228)This crate is also Unicode aware by default, which means that `\d` might match
[229](https://docs.rs#229)more than you might expect it to. For example:
[230](https://docs.rs#230)
[231](https://docs.rs#231)```rust
[232](https://docs.rs#232)use regex::Regex;
[233](https://docs.rs#233)
[234](https://docs.rs#234)let re = Regex::new(r"^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$").unwrap();
[235](https://docs.rs#235)assert!(re.is_match("𝟚𝟘𝟙𝟘-𝟘𝟛-𝟙𝟜"));
[236](https://docs.rs#236)```
[237](https://docs.rs#237)
[238](https://docs.rs#238)To only match an ASCII decimal digit, all of the following are equivalent:
[239](https://docs.rs#239)
[240](https://docs.rs#240)* `[0-9]`
[241](https://docs.rs#241)* `(?-u:\d)`
[242](https://docs.rs#242)* `[[:digit:]]`
[243](https://docs.rs#243)* `[\d&&\p{ascii}]`
[244](https://docs.rs#244)
[245](https://docs.rs#245)### Example: finding dates in a haystack
[246](https://docs.rs#246)
[247](https://docs.rs#247)In the previous example, we showed how one might validate that a haystack,
[248](https://docs.rs#248)in its entirety, corresponded to a particular date format. But what if we wanted
[249](https://docs.rs#249)to extract all things that look like dates in a specific format from a haystack?
[250](https://docs.rs#250)To do this, we can use an iterator API to find all matches (notice that we've
[251](https://docs.rs#251)removed the anchors and switched to looking for ASCII-only digits):
[252](https://docs.rs#252)
[253](https://docs.rs#253)```rust
[254](https://docs.rs#254)use regex::Regex;
[255](https://docs.rs#255)
[256](https://docs.rs#256)let re = Regex::new(r"[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}").unwrap();
[257](https://docs.rs#257)let hay = "What do 1865-04-14, 1881-07-02, 1901-09-06 and 1963-11-22 have in common?";
[258](https://docs.rs#258)// 'm' is a 'Match', and 'as_str()' returns the matching part of the haystack.
[259](https://docs.rs#259)let dates: Vec<&str> = re.find_iter(hay).map(|m| m.as_str()).collect();
[260](https://docs.rs#260)assert_eq!(dates, vec![
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    "1865-04-14",
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    "1881-07-02",
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    "1901-09-06",
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    "1963-11-22",
[265](https://docs.rs#265)]);
[266](https://docs.rs#266)```
[267](https://docs.rs#267)
[268](https://docs.rs#268)We can also iterate over [`Captures`] values instead of [`Match`] values, and
[269](https://docs.rs#269)that in turn permits accessing each component of the date via capturing groups:
[270](https://docs.rs#270)
[271](https://docs.rs#271)```rust
[272](https://docs.rs#272)use regex::Regex;
[273](https://docs.rs#273)
[274](https://docs.rs#274)let re = Regex::new(r"(?<y>[0-9]{4})-(?<m>[0-9]{2})-(?<d>[0-9]{2})").unwrap();
[275](https://docs.rs#275)let hay = "What do 1865-04-14, 1881-07-02, 1901-09-06 and 1963-11-22 have in common?";
[276](https://docs.rs#276)// 'm' is a 'Match', and 'as_str()' returns the matching part of the haystack.
[277](https://docs.rs#277)let dates: Vec<(&str, &str, &str)> = re.captures_iter(hay).map(|caps| {
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    // The unwraps are okay because every capture group must match if the whole
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    // regex matches, and in this context, we know we have a match.
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    //
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    // Note that we use `caps.name("y").unwrap().as_str()` instead of
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    // `&caps["y"]` because the lifetime of the former is the same as the
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    // lifetime of `hay` above, but the lifetime of the latter is tied to the
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    // lifetime of `caps` due to how the `Index` trait is defined.
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    let year = caps.name("y").unwrap().as_str();
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    let month = caps.name("m").unwrap().as_str();
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    let day = caps.name("d").unwrap().as_str();
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    (year, month, day)
[289](https://docs.rs#289)}).collect();
[290](https://docs.rs#290)assert_eq!(dates, vec![
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    ("1865", "04", "14"),
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    ("1881", "07", "02"),
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    ("1901", "09", "06"),
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    ("1963", "11", "22"),
[295](https://docs.rs#295)]);
[296](https://docs.rs#296)```
[297](https://docs.rs#297)
[298](https://docs.rs#298)### Example: simpler capture group extraction
[299](https://docs.rs#299)
[300](https://docs.rs#300)One can use [`Captures::extract`] to make the code from the previous example a
[301](https://docs.rs#301)bit simpler in this case:
[302](https://docs.rs#302)
[303](https://docs.rs#303)```rust
[304](https://docs.rs#304)use regex::Regex;
[305](https://docs.rs#305)
[306](https://docs.rs#306)let re = Regex::new(r"([0-9]{4})-([0-9]{2})-([0-9]{2})").unwrap();
[307](https://docs.rs#307)let hay = "What do 1865-04-14, 1881-07-02, 1901-09-06 and 1963-11-22 have in common?";
[308](https://docs.rs#308)let dates: Vec<(&str, &str, &str)> = re.captures_iter(hay).map(|caps| {
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    let (_, [year, month, day]) = caps.extract();
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    (year, month, day)
[311](https://docs.rs#311)}).collect();
[312](https://docs.rs#312)assert_eq!(dates, vec![
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    ("1865", "04", "14"),
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    ("1881", "07", "02"),
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    ("1901", "09", "06"),
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    ("1963", "11", "22"),
[317](https://docs.rs#317)]);
[318](https://docs.rs#318)```
[319](https://docs.rs#319)
[320](https://docs.rs#320)`Captures::extract` works by ensuring that the number of matching groups match
[321](https://docs.rs#321)the number of groups requested via the `[year, month, day]` syntax. If they do,
[322](https://docs.rs#322)then the substrings for each corresponding capture group are automatically
[323](https://docs.rs#323)returned in an appropriately sized array. Rust's syntax for pattern matching
[324](https://docs.rs#324)arrays does the rest.
[325](https://docs.rs#325)
[326](https://docs.rs#326)### Example: replacement with named capture groups
[327](https://docs.rs#327)
[328](https://docs.rs#328)Building on the previous example, perhaps we'd like to rearrange the date
[329](https://docs.rs#329)formats. This can be done by finding each match and replacing it with
[330](https://docs.rs#330)something different. The [`Regex::replace_all`] routine provides a convenient
[331](https://docs.rs#331)way to do this, including by supporting references to named groups in the
[332](https://docs.rs#332)replacement string:
[333](https://docs.rs#333)
[334](https://docs.rs#334)```rust
[335](https://docs.rs#335)use regex::Regex;
[336](https://docs.rs#336)
[337](https://docs.rs#337)let re = Regex::new(r"(?<y>\d{4})-(?<m>\d{2})-(?<d>\d{2})").unwrap();
[338](https://docs.rs#338)let before = "1973-01-05, 1975-08-25 and 1980-10-18";
[339](https://docs.rs#339)let after = re.replace_all(before, "$m/$d/$y");
[340](https://docs.rs#340)assert_eq!(after, "01/05/1973, 08/25/1975 and 10/18/1980");
[341](https://docs.rs#341)```
[342](https://docs.rs#342)
[343](https://docs.rs#343)The replace methods are actually polymorphic in the replacement, which
[344](https://docs.rs#344)provides more flexibility than is seen here. (See the documentation for
[345](https://docs.rs#345)[`Regex::replace`] for more details.)
[346](https://docs.rs#346)
[347](https://docs.rs#347)### Example: verbose mode
[348](https://docs.rs#348)
[349](https://docs.rs#349)When your regex gets complicated, you might consider using something other
[350](https://docs.rs#350)than regex. But if you stick with regex, you can use the `x` flag to enable
[351](https://docs.rs#351)insignificant whitespace mode or "verbose mode." In this mode, whitespace
[352](https://docs.rs#352)is treated as insignificant and one may write comments. This may make your
[353](https://docs.rs#353)patterns easier to comprehend.
[354](https://docs.rs#354)
[355](https://docs.rs#355)```rust
[356](https://docs.rs#356)use regex::Regex;
[357](https://docs.rs#357)
[358](https://docs.rs#358)let re = Regex::new(r"(?x)
[359](https://docs.rs#359)  (?P<y>\d{4}) # the year, including all Unicode digits
[360](https://docs.rs#360)  -
[361](https://docs.rs#361)  (?P<m>\d{2}) # the month, including all Unicode digits
[362](https://docs.rs#362)  -
[363](https://docs.rs#363)  (?P<d>\d{2}) # the day, including all Unicode digits
[364](https://docs.rs#364)").unwrap();
[365](https://docs.rs#365)
[366](https://docs.rs#366)let before = "1973-01-05, 1975-08-25 and 1980-10-18";
[367](https://docs.rs#367)let after = re.replace_all(before, "$m/$d/$y");
[368](https://docs.rs#368)assert_eq!(after, "01/05/1973, 08/25/1975 and 10/18/1980");
[369](https://docs.rs#369)```
[370](https://docs.rs#370)
[371](https://docs.rs#371)If you wish to match against whitespace in this mode, you can still use `\s`,
[372](https://docs.rs#372)`\n`, `\t`, etc. For escaping a single space character, you can escape it
[373](https://docs.rs#373)directly with `\ `, use its hex character code `\x20` or temporarily disable
[374](https://docs.rs#374)the `x` flag, e.g., `(?-x: )`.
[375](https://docs.rs#375)
[376](https://docs.rs#376)### Example: match multiple regular expressions simultaneously
[377](https://docs.rs#377)
[378](https://docs.rs#378)This demonstrates how to use a [`RegexSet`] to match multiple (possibly
[379](https://docs.rs#379)overlapping) regexes in a single scan of a haystack:
[380](https://docs.rs#380)
[381](https://docs.rs#381)```rust
[382](https://docs.rs#382)use regex::RegexSet;
[383](https://docs.rs#383)
[384](https://docs.rs#384)let set = RegexSet::new(&[
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    r"\w+",
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    r"\d+",
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    r"\pL+",
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    r"foo",
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    r"bar",
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    r"barfoo",
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    r"foobar",
[392](https://docs.rs#392)]).unwrap();
[393](https://docs.rs#393)
[394](https://docs.rs#394)// Iterate over and collect all of the matches. Each match corresponds to the
[395](https://docs.rs#395)// ID of the matching pattern.
[396](https://docs.rs#396)let matches: Vec<_> = set.matches("foobar").into_iter().collect();
[397](https://docs.rs#397)assert_eq!(matches, vec![0, 2, 3, 4, 6]);
[398](https://docs.rs#398)
[399](https://docs.rs#399)// You can also test whether a particular regex matched:
[400](https://docs.rs#400)let matches = set.matches("foobar");
[401](https://docs.rs#401)assert!(!matches.matched(5));
[402](https://docs.rs#402)assert!(matches.matched(6));
[403](https://docs.rs#403)```
[404](https://docs.rs#404)
[405](https://docs.rs#405)# Performance
[406](https://docs.rs#406)
[407](https://docs.rs#407)This section briefly discusses a few concerns regarding the speed and resource
[408](https://docs.rs#408)usage of regexes.
[409](https://docs.rs#409)
[410](https://docs.rs#410)### Only ask for what you need
[411](https://docs.rs#411)
[412](https://docs.rs#412)When running a search with a regex, there are generally three different types
[413](https://docs.rs#413)of information one can ask for:
[414](https://docs.rs#414)
[415](https://docs.rs#415)1. Does a regex match in a haystack?
[416](https://docs.rs#416)2. Where does a regex match in a haystack?
[417](https://docs.rs#417)3. Where do each of the capturing groups match in a haystack?
[418](https://docs.rs#418)
[419](https://docs.rs#419)Generally speaking, this crate could provide a function to answer only #3,
[420](https://docs.rs#420)which would subsume #1 and #2 automatically. However, it can be significantly
[421](https://docs.rs#421)more expensive to compute the location of capturing group matches, so it's best
[422](https://docs.rs#422)not to do it if you don't need to.
[423](https://docs.rs#423)
[424](https://docs.rs#424)Therefore, only ask for what you need. For example, don't use [`Regex::find`]
[425](https://docs.rs#425)if you only need to test if a regex matches a haystack. Use [`Regex::is_match`]
[426](https://docs.rs#426)instead.
[427](https://docs.rs#427)
[428](https://docs.rs#428)### Unicode can impact memory usage and search speed
[429](https://docs.rs#429)
[430](https://docs.rs#430)This crate has first class support for Unicode and it is **enabled by default**.
[431](https://docs.rs#431)In many cases, the extra memory required to support it will be negligible and
[432](https://docs.rs#432)it typically won't impact search speed. But it can in some cases.
[433](https://docs.rs#433)
[434](https://docs.rs#434)With respect to memory usage, the impact of Unicode principally manifests
[435](https://docs.rs#435)through the use of Unicode character classes. Unicode character classes
[436](https://docs.rs#436)tend to be quite large. For example, `\w` by default matches around 140,000
[437](https://docs.rs#437)distinct codepoints. This requires additional memory, and tends to slow down
[438](https://docs.rs#438)regex compilation. While a `\w` here and there is unlikely to be noticed,
[439](https://docs.rs#439)writing `\w{100}` will for example result in quite a large regex by default.
[440](https://docs.rs#440)Indeed, `\w` is considerably larger than its ASCII-only version, so if your
[441](https://docs.rs#441)requirements are satisfied by ASCII, it's probably a good idea to stick to
[442](https://docs.rs#442)ASCII classes. The ASCII-only version of `\w` can be spelled in a number of
[443](https://docs.rs#443)ways. All of the following are equivalent:
[444](https://docs.rs#444)
[445](https://docs.rs#445)* `[0-9A-Za-z_]`
[446](https://docs.rs#446)* `(?-u:\w)`
[447](https://docs.rs#447)* `[[:word:]]`
[448](https://docs.rs#448)* `[\w&&\p{ascii}]`
[449](https://docs.rs#449)
[450](https://docs.rs#450)With respect to search speed, Unicode tends to be handled pretty well, even when
[451](https://docs.rs#451)using large Unicode character classes. However, some of the faster internal
[452](https://docs.rs#452)regex engines cannot handle a Unicode aware word boundary assertion. So if you
[453](https://docs.rs#453)don't need Unicode-aware word boundary assertions, you might consider using
[454](https://docs.rs#454)`(?-u:\b)` instead of `\b`, where the former uses an ASCII-only definition of
[455](https://docs.rs#455)a word character.
[456](https://docs.rs#456)
[457](https://docs.rs#457)### Literals might accelerate searches
[458](https://docs.rs#458)
[459](https://docs.rs#459)This crate tends to be quite good at recognizing literals in a regex pattern
[460](https://docs.rs#460)and using them to accelerate a search. If it is at all possible to include
[461](https://docs.rs#461)some kind of literal in your pattern, then it might make search substantially
[462](https://docs.rs#462)faster. For example, in the regex `\w+@\w+`, the engine will look for
[463](https://docs.rs#463)occurrences of `@` and then try a reverse match for `\w+` to find the start
[464](https://docs.rs#464)position.
[465](https://docs.rs#465)
[466](https://docs.rs#466)### Avoid re-compiling regexes, especially in a loop
[467](https://docs.rs#467)
[468](https://docs.rs#468)It is an anti-pattern to compile the same pattern in a loop since regex
[469](https://docs.rs#469)compilation is typically expensive. (It takes anywhere from a few microseconds
[470](https://docs.rs#470)to a few **milliseconds** depending on the size of the pattern.) Not only is
[471](https://docs.rs#471)compilation itself expensive, but this also prevents optimizations that reuse
[472](https://docs.rs#472)allocations internally to the regex engine.
[473](https://docs.rs#473)
[474](https://docs.rs#474)In Rust, it can sometimes be a pain to pass regular expressions around if
[475](https://docs.rs#475)they're used from inside a helper function. Instead, we recommend using
[476](https://docs.rs#476)[`std::sync::LazyLock`], or the [`once_cell`] crate,
[477](https://docs.rs#477)if you can't use the standard library.
[478](https://docs.rs#478)
[479](https://docs.rs#479)This example shows how to use `std::sync::LazyLock`:
[480](https://docs.rs#480)
[481](https://docs.rs#481)```rust
[482](https://docs.rs#482)use std::sync::LazyLock;
[483](https://docs.rs#483)
[484](https://docs.rs#484)use regex::Regex;
[485](https://docs.rs#485)
[486](https://docs.rs#486)fn some_helper_function(haystack: &str) -> bool {
[487](https://docs.rs#487)    static RE: LazyLock<Regex> = LazyLock::new(|| Regex::new(r"...").unwrap());
[488](https://docs.rs#488)    RE.is_match(haystack)
[489](https://docs.rs#489)}
[490](https://docs.rs#490)
[491](https://docs.rs#491)fn main() {
[492](https://docs.rs#492)    assert!(some_helper_function("abc"));
[493](https://docs.rs#493)    assert!(!some_helper_function("ac"));
[494](https://docs.rs#494)}
[495](https://docs.rs#495)```
[496](https://docs.rs#496)
[497](https://docs.rs#497)Specifically, in this example, the regex will be compiled when it is used for
[498](https://docs.rs#498)the first time. On subsequent uses, it will reuse the previously built `Regex`.
[499](https://docs.rs#499)Notice how one can define the `Regex` locally to a specific function.
[500](https://docs.rs#500)
[501](https://docs.rs#501)[`std::sync::LazyLock`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.LazyLock.html
[502](https://docs.rs#502)[`once_cell`]: https://crates.io/crates/once_cell
[503](https://docs.rs#503)
[504](https://docs.rs#504)### Sharing a regex across threads can result in contention
[505](https://docs.rs#505)
[506](https://docs.rs#506)While a single `Regex` can be freely used from multiple threads simultaneously,
[507](https://docs.rs#507)there is a small synchronization cost that must be paid. Generally speaking,
[508](https://docs.rs#508)one shouldn't expect to observe this unless the principal task in each thread
[509](https://docs.rs#509)is searching with the regex *and* most searches are on short haystacks. In this
[510](https://docs.rs#510)case, internal contention on shared resources can spike and increase latency,
[511](https://docs.rs#511)which in turn may slow down each individual search.
[512](https://docs.rs#512)
[513](https://docs.rs#513)One can work around this by cloning each `Regex` before sending it to another
[514](https://docs.rs#514)thread. The cloned regexes will still share the same internal read-only portion
[515](https://docs.rs#515)of its compiled state (it's reference counted), but each thread will get
[516](https://docs.rs#516)optimized access to the mutable space that is used to run a search. In general,
[517](https://docs.rs#517)there is no additional cost in memory to doing this. The only cost is the added
[518](https://docs.rs#518)code complexity required to explicitly clone the regex. (If you share the same
[519](https://docs.rs#519)`Regex` across multiple threads, each thread still gets its own mutable space,
[520](https://docs.rs#520)but accessing that space is slower.)
[521](https://docs.rs#521)
[522](https://docs.rs#522)# Unicode
[523](https://docs.rs#523)
[524](https://docs.rs#524)This section discusses what kind of Unicode support this regex library has.
[525](https://docs.rs#525)Before showing some examples, we'll summarize the relevant points:
[526](https://docs.rs#526)
[527](https://docs.rs#527)* This crate almost fully implements "Basic Unicode Support" (Level 1) as
[528](https://docs.rs#528)specified by the [Unicode Technical Standard #18][UTS18]. The full details
[529](https://docs.rs#529)of what is supported are documented in [UNICODE.md] in the root of the regex
[530](https://docs.rs#530)crate repository. There is virtually no support for "Extended Unicode Support"
[531](https://docs.rs#531)(Level 2) from UTS#18.
[532](https://docs.rs#532)* The top-level [`Regex`] runs searches *as if* iterating over each of the
[533](https://docs.rs#533)codepoints in the haystack. That is, the fundamental atom of matching is a
[534](https://docs.rs#534)single codepoint.
[535](https://docs.rs#535)* [`bytes::Regex`], in contrast, permits disabling Unicode mode for part of all
[536](https://docs.rs#536)of your pattern in all cases. When Unicode mode is disabled, then a search is
[537](https://docs.rs#537)run *as if* iterating over each byte in the haystack. That is, the fundamental
[538](https://docs.rs#538)atom of matching is a single byte. (A top-level `Regex` also permits disabling
[539](https://docs.rs#539)Unicode and thus matching *as if* it were one byte at a time, but only when
[540](https://docs.rs#540)doing so wouldn't permit matching invalid UTF-8.)
[541](https://docs.rs#541)* When Unicode mode is enabled (the default), `.` will match an entire Unicode
[542](https://docs.rs#542)scalar value, even when it is encoded using multiple bytes. When Unicode mode
[543](https://docs.rs#543)is disabled (e.g., `(?-u:.)`), then `.` will match a single byte in all cases.
[544](https://docs.rs#544)* The character classes `\w`, `\d` and `\s` are all Unicode-aware by default.
[545](https://docs.rs#545)Use `(?-u:\w)`, `(?-u:\d)` and `(?-u:\s)` to get their ASCII-only definitions.
[546](https://docs.rs#546)* Similarly, `\b` and `\B` use a Unicode definition of a "word" character.
[547](https://docs.rs#547)To get ASCII-only word boundaries, use `(?-u:\b)` and `(?-u:\B)`. This also
[548](https://docs.rs#548)applies to the special word boundary assertions. (That is, `\b{start}`,
[549](https://docs.rs#549)`\b{end}`, `\b{start-half}`, `\b{end-half}`.)
[550](https://docs.rs#550)* `^` and `$` are **not** Unicode-aware in multi-line mode. Namely, they only
[551](https://docs.rs#551)recognize `\n` (assuming CRLF mode is not enabled) and not any of the other
[552](https://docs.rs#552)forms of line terminators defined by Unicode.
[553](https://docs.rs#553)* Case insensitive searching is Unicode-aware and uses simple case folding.
[554](https://docs.rs#554)* Unicode general categories, scripts and many boolean properties are available
[555](https://docs.rs#555)by default via the `\p{property name}` syntax.
[556](https://docs.rs#556)* In all cases, matches are reported using byte offsets. Or more precisely,
[557](https://docs.rs#557)UTF-8 code unit offsets. This permits constant time indexing and slicing of the
[558](https://docs.rs#558)haystack.
[559](https://docs.rs#559)
[560](https://docs.rs#560)[UTS18]: https://unicode.org/reports/tr18/
[561](https://docs.rs#561)[UNICODE.md]: https://github.com/rust-lang/regex/blob/master/UNICODE.md
[562](https://docs.rs#562)
[563](https://docs.rs#563)Patterns themselves are **only** interpreted as a sequence of Unicode scalar
[564](https://docs.rs#564)values. This means you can use Unicode characters directly in your pattern:
[565](https://docs.rs#565)
[566](https://docs.rs#566)```rust
[567](https://docs.rs#567)use regex::Regex;
[568](https://docs.rs#568)
[569](https://docs.rs#569)let re = Regex::new(r"(?i)Δ+").unwrap();
[570](https://docs.rs#570)let m = re.find("ΔδΔ").unwrap();
[571](https://docs.rs#571)assert_eq!((0, 6), (m.start(), m.end()));
[572](https://docs.rs#572)// alternatively:
[573](https://docs.rs#573)assert_eq!(0..6, m.range());
[574](https://docs.rs#574)```
[575](https://docs.rs#575)
[576](https://docs.rs#576)As noted above, Unicode general categories, scripts, script extensions, ages
[577](https://docs.rs#577)and a smattering of boolean properties are available as character classes. For
[578](https://docs.rs#578)example, you can match a sequence of numerals, Greek or Cherokee letters:
[579](https://docs.rs#579)
[580](https://docs.rs#580)```rust
[581](https://docs.rs#581)use regex::Regex;
[582](https://docs.rs#582)
[583](https://docs.rs#583)let re = Regex::new(r"[\pN\p{Greek}\p{Cherokee}]+").unwrap();
[584](https://docs.rs#584)let m = re.find("abcΔᎠβⅠᏴγδⅡxyz").unwrap();
[585](https://docs.rs#585)assert_eq!(3..23, m.range());
[586](https://docs.rs#586)```
[587](https://docs.rs#587)
[588](https://docs.rs#588)While not specific to Unicode, this library also supports character class set
[589](https://docs.rs#589)operations. Namely, one can nest character classes arbitrarily and perform set
[590](https://docs.rs#590)operations on them. Those set operations are union (the default), intersection,
[591](https://docs.rs#591)difference and symmetric difference. These set operations tend to be most
[592](https://docs.rs#592)useful with Unicode character classes. For example, to match any codepoint
[593](https://docs.rs#593)that is both in the `Greek` script and in the `Letter` general category:
[594](https://docs.rs#594)
[595](https://docs.rs#595)```rust
[596](https://docs.rs#596)use regex::Regex;
[597](https://docs.rs#597)
[598](https://docs.rs#598)let re = Regex::new(r"[\p{Greek}&&\pL]+").unwrap();
[599](https://docs.rs#599)let subs: Vec<&str> = re.find_iter("ΔδΔ𐅌ΔδΔ").map(|m| m.as_str()).collect();
[600](https://docs.rs#600)assert_eq!(subs, vec!["ΔδΔ", "ΔδΔ"]);
[601](https://docs.rs#601)
[602](https://docs.rs#602)// If we just matches on Greek, then all codepoints would match!
[603](https://docs.rs#603)let re = Regex::new(r"\p{Greek}+").unwrap();
[604](https://docs.rs#604)let subs: Vec<&str> = re.find_iter("ΔδΔ𐅌ΔδΔ").map(|m| m.as_str()).collect();
[605](https://docs.rs#605)assert_eq!(subs, vec!["ΔδΔ𐅌ΔδΔ"]);
[606](https://docs.rs#606)```
[607](https://docs.rs#607)
[608](https://docs.rs#608)### Opt out of Unicode support
[609](https://docs.rs#609)
[610](https://docs.rs#610)The [`bytes::Regex`] type that can be used to search `&[u8]` haystacks. By
[611](https://docs.rs#611)default, haystacks are conventionally treated as UTF-8 just like it is with the
[612](https://docs.rs#612)main `Regex` type. However, this behavior can be disabled by turning off the
[613](https://docs.rs#613)`u` flag, even if doing so could result in matching invalid UTF-8. For example,
[614](https://docs.rs#614)when the `u` flag is disabled, `.` will match any byte instead of any Unicode
[615](https://docs.rs#615)scalar value.
[616](https://docs.rs#616)
[617](https://docs.rs#617)Disabling the `u` flag is also possible with the standard `&str`-based `Regex`
[618](https://docs.rs#618)type, but it is only allowed where the UTF-8 invariant is maintained. For
[619](https://docs.rs#619)example, `(?-u:\w)` is an ASCII-only `\w` character class and is legal in an
[620](https://docs.rs#620)`&str`-based `Regex`, but `(?-u:\W)` will attempt to match *any byte* that
[621](https://docs.rs#621)isn't in `(?-u:\w)`, which in turn includes bytes that are invalid UTF-8.
[622](https://docs.rs#622)Similarly, `(?-u:\xFF)` will attempt to match the raw byte `\xFF` (instead of
[623](https://docs.rs#623)`U+00FF`), which is invalid UTF-8 and therefore is illegal in `&str`-based
[624](https://docs.rs#624)regexes.
[625](https://docs.rs#625)
[626](https://docs.rs#626)Finally, since Unicode support requires bundling large Unicode data
[627](https://docs.rs#627)tables, this crate exposes knobs to disable the compilation of those
[628](https://docs.rs#628)data tables, which can be useful for shrinking binary size and reducing
[629](https://docs.rs#629)compilation times. For details on how to do that, see the section on [crate
[630](https://docs.rs#630)features](#crate-features).
[631](https://docs.rs#631)
[632](https://docs.rs#632)# Syntax
[633](https://docs.rs#633)
[634](https://docs.rs#634)The syntax supported in this crate is documented below.
[635](https://docs.rs#635)
[636](https://docs.rs#636)Note that the regular expression parser and abstract syntax are exposed in
[637](https://docs.rs#637)a separate crate, [`regex-syntax`](https://docs.rs/regex-syntax).
[638](https://docs.rs#638)
[639](https://docs.rs#639)### Matching one character
[640](https://docs.rs#640)
[641](https://docs.rs#641)<pre class="rust">
[642](https://docs.rs#642).             any character except new line (includes new line with s flag)
[643](https://docs.rs#643)[0-9]         any ASCII digit
[644](https://docs.rs#644)\d            digit (\p{Nd})
[645](https://docs.rs#645)\D            not digit
[646](https://docs.rs#646)\pX           Unicode character class identified by a one-letter name
[647](https://docs.rs#647)\p{Greek}     Unicode character class (general category or script)
[648](https://docs.rs#648)\PX           Negated Unicode character class identified by a one-letter name
[649](https://docs.rs#649)\P{Greek}     negated Unicode character class (general category or script)
[650](https://docs.rs#650)</pre>
[651](https://docs.rs#651)
[652](https://docs.rs#652)### Character classes
[653](https://docs.rs#653)
[654](https://docs.rs#654)<pre class="rust">
[655](https://docs.rs#655)[xyz]         A character class matching either x, y or z (union).
[656](https://docs.rs#656)[^xyz]        A character class matching any character except x, y and z.
[657](https://docs.rs#657)[a-z]         A character class matching any character in range a-z.
[658](https://docs.rs#658)[[:alpha:]]   ASCII character class ([A-Za-z])
[659](https://docs.rs#659)[[:^alpha:]]  Negated ASCII character class ([^A-Za-z])
[660](https://docs.rs#660)[x[^xyz]]     Nested/grouping character class (matching any character except y and z)
[661](https://docs.rs#661)[a-y&&xyz]    Intersection (matching x or y)
[662](https://docs.rs#662)[0-9&&[^4]]   Subtraction using intersection and negation (matching 0-9 except 4)
[663](https://docs.rs#663)[0-9--4]      Direct subtraction (matching 0-9 except 4)
[664](https://docs.rs#664)[a-g~~b-h]    Symmetric difference (matching `a` and `h` only)
[665](https://docs.rs#665)[\[\]]        Escaping in character classes (matching [ or ])
[666](https://docs.rs#666)[a&&b]        An empty character class matching nothing
[667](https://docs.rs#667)</pre>
[668](https://docs.rs#668)
[669](https://docs.rs#669)Any named character class may appear inside a bracketed `[...]` character
[670](https://docs.rs#670)class. For example, `[\p{Greek}[:digit:]]` matches any ASCII digit or any
[671](https://docs.rs#671)codepoint in the `Greek` script. `[\p{Greek}&&\pL]` matches Greek letters.
[672](https://docs.rs#672)
[673](https://docs.rs#673)Precedence in character classes, from most binding to least:
[674](https://docs.rs#674)
[675](https://docs.rs#675)1. Ranges: `[a-cd]` == `[[a-c]d]`
[676](https://docs.rs#676)2. Union: `[ab&&bc]` == `[[ab]&&[bc]]`
[677](https://docs.rs#677)3. Intersection, difference, symmetric difference. All three have equivalent
[678](https://docs.rs#678)precedence, and are evaluated in left-to-right order. For example,
[679](https://docs.rs#679)`[\pL--\p{Greek}&&\p{Uppercase}]` == `[[\pL--\p{Greek}]&&\p{Uppercase}]`.
[680](https://docs.rs#680)4. Negation: `[^a-z&&b]` == `[^[a-z&&b]]`.
[681](https://docs.rs#681)
[682](https://docs.rs#682)### Composites
[683](https://docs.rs#683)
[684](https://docs.rs#684)<pre class="rust">
[685](https://docs.rs#685)xy    concatenation (x followed by y)
[686](https://docs.rs#686)x|y   alternation (x or y, prefer x)
[687](https://docs.rs#687)</pre>
[688](https://docs.rs#688)
[689](https://docs.rs#689)This example shows how an alternation works, and what it means to prefer a
[690](https://docs.rs#690)branch in the alternation over subsequent branches.
[691](https://docs.rs#691)
[692](https://docs.rs#692)```
[693](https://docs.rs#693)use regex::Regex;
[694](https://docs.rs#694)
[695](https://docs.rs#695)let haystack = "samwise";
[696](https://docs.rs#696)// If 'samwise' comes first in our alternation, then it is
[697](https://docs.rs#697)// preferred as a match, even if the regex engine could
[698](https://docs.rs#698)// technically detect that 'sam' led to a match earlier.
[699](https://docs.rs#699)let re = Regex::new(r"samwise|sam").unwrap();
[700](https://docs.rs#700)assert_eq!("samwise", re.find(haystack).unwrap().as_str());
[701](https://docs.rs#701)// But if 'sam' comes first, then it will match instead.
[702](https://docs.rs#702)// In this case, it is impossible for 'samwise' to match
[703](https://docs.rs#703)// because 'sam' is a prefix of it.
[704](https://docs.rs#704)let re = Regex::new(r"sam|samwise").unwrap();
[705](https://docs.rs#705)assert_eq!("sam", re.find(haystack).unwrap().as_str());
[706](https://docs.rs#706)```
[707](https://docs.rs#707)
[708](https://docs.rs#708)### Repetitions
[709](https://docs.rs#709)
[710](https://docs.rs#710)<pre class="rust">
[711](https://docs.rs#711)x*        zero or more of x (greedy)
[712](https://docs.rs#712)x+        one or more of x (greedy)
[713](https://docs.rs#713)x?        zero or one of x (greedy)
[714](https://docs.rs#714)x*?       zero or more of x (ungreedy/lazy)
[715](https://docs.rs#715)x+?       one or more of x (ungreedy/lazy)
[716](https://docs.rs#716)x??       zero or one of x (ungreedy/lazy)
[717](https://docs.rs#717)x{n,m}    at least n x and at most m x (greedy)
[718](https://docs.rs#718)x{n,}     at least n x (greedy)
[719](https://docs.rs#719)x{n}      exactly n x
[720](https://docs.rs#720)x{n,m}?   at least n x and at most m x (ungreedy/lazy)
[721](https://docs.rs#721)x{n,}?    at least n x (ungreedy/lazy)
[722](https://docs.rs#722)x{n}?     exactly n x
[723](https://docs.rs#723)</pre>
[724](https://docs.rs#724)
[725](https://docs.rs#725)### Empty matches
[726](https://docs.rs#726)
[727](https://docs.rs#727)<pre class="rust">
[728](https://docs.rs#728)^               the beginning of a haystack (or start-of-line with multi-line mode)
[729](https://docs.rs#729)$               the end of a haystack (or end-of-line with multi-line mode)
[730](https://docs.rs#730)\A              only the beginning of a haystack (even with multi-line mode enabled)
[731](https://docs.rs#731)\z              only the end of a haystack (even with multi-line mode enabled)
[732](https://docs.rs#732)\b              a Unicode word boundary (\w on one side and \W, \A, or \z on other)
[733](https://docs.rs#733)\B              not a Unicode word boundary
[734](https://docs.rs#734)\b{start}, \<   a Unicode start-of-word boundary (\W|\A on the left, \w on the right)
[735](https://docs.rs#735)\b{end}, \>     a Unicode end-of-word boundary (\w on the left, \W|\z on the right))
[736](https://docs.rs#736)\b{start-half}  half of a Unicode start-of-word boundary (\W|\A on the left)
[737](https://docs.rs#737)\b{end-half}    half of a Unicode end-of-word boundary (\W|\z on the right)
[738](https://docs.rs#738)</pre>
[739](https://docs.rs#739)
[740](https://docs.rs#740)The empty regex is valid and matches the empty string. For example, the
[741](https://docs.rs#741)empty regex matches `abc` at positions `0`, `1`, `2` and `3`. When using the
[742](https://docs.rs#742)top-level [`Regex`] on `&str` haystacks, an empty match that splits a codepoint
[743](https://docs.rs#743)is guaranteed to never be returned. However, such matches are permitted when
[744](https://docs.rs#744)using a [`bytes::Regex`]. For example:
[745](https://docs.rs#745)
[746](https://docs.rs#746)```rust
[747](https://docs.rs#747)let re = regex::Regex::new(r"").unwrap();
[748](https://docs.rs#748)let ranges: Vec<_> = re.find_iter("💩").map(|m| m.range()).collect();
[749](https://docs.rs#749)assert_eq!(ranges, vec![0..0, 4..4]);
[750](https://docs.rs#750)
[751](https://docs.rs#751)let re = regex::bytes::Regex::new(r"").unwrap();
[752](https://docs.rs#752)let ranges: Vec<_> = re.find_iter("💩".as_bytes()).map(|m| m.range()).collect();
[753](https://docs.rs#753)assert_eq!(ranges, vec![0..0, 1..1, 2..2, 3..3, 4..4]);
[754](https://docs.rs#754)```
[755](https://docs.rs#755)
[756](https://docs.rs#756)Note that an empty regex is distinct from a regex that can never match.
[757](https://docs.rs#757)For example, the regex `[a&&b]` is a character class that represents the
[758](https://docs.rs#758)intersection of `a` and `b`. That intersection is empty, which means the
[759](https://docs.rs#759)character class is empty. Since nothing is in the empty set, `[a&&b]` matches
[760](https://docs.rs#760)nothing, not even the empty string.
[761](https://docs.rs#761)
[762](https://docs.rs#762)### Grouping and flags
[763](https://docs.rs#763)
[764](https://docs.rs#764)<pre class="rust">
[765](https://docs.rs#765)(exp)          numbered capture group (indexed by opening parenthesis)
[766](https://docs.rs#766)(?P<name>exp)  named (also numbered) capture group (names must be alpha-numeric)
[767](https://docs.rs#767)(?<name>exp)   named (also numbered) capture group (names must be alpha-numeric)
[768](https://docs.rs#768)(?:exp)        non-capturing group
[769](https://docs.rs#769)(?flags)       set flags within current group
[770](https://docs.rs#770)(?flags:exp)   set flags for exp (non-capturing)
[771](https://docs.rs#771)</pre>
[772](https://docs.rs#772)
[773](https://docs.rs#773)Capture group names must be any sequence of alpha-numeric Unicode codepoints,
[774](https://docs.rs#774)in addition to `.`, `_`, `[` and `]`. Names must start with either an `_` or
[775](https://docs.rs#775)an alphabetic codepoint. Alphabetic codepoints correspond to the `Alphabetic`
[776](https://docs.rs#776)Unicode property, while numeric codepoints correspond to the union of the
[777](https://docs.rs#777)`Decimal_Number`, `Letter_Number` and `Other_Number` general categories.
[778](https://docs.rs#778)
[779](https://docs.rs#779)Flags are each a single character. For example, `(?x)` sets the flag `x`
[780](https://docs.rs#780)and `(?-x)` clears the flag `x`. Multiple flags can be set or cleared at
[781](https://docs.rs#781)the same time: `(?xy)` sets both the `x` and `y` flags and `(?x-y)` sets
[782](https://docs.rs#782)the `x` flag and clears the `y` flag.
[783](https://docs.rs#783)
[784](https://docs.rs#784)All flags are by default disabled unless stated otherwise. They are:
[785](https://docs.rs#785)
[786](https://docs.rs#786)<pre class="rust">
[787](https://docs.rs#787)i     case-insensitive: letters match both upper and lower case
[788](https://docs.rs#788)m     multi-line mode: ^ and $ match begin/end of line
[789](https://docs.rs#789)s     allow . to match \n
[790](https://docs.rs#790)R     enables CRLF mode: when multi-line mode is enabled, \r\n is used
[791](https://docs.rs#791)U     swap the meaning of x* and x*?
[792](https://docs.rs#792)u     Unicode support (enabled by default)
[793](https://docs.rs#793)x     verbose mode, ignores whitespace and allow line comments (starting with `#`)
[794](https://docs.rs#794)</pre>
[795](https://docs.rs#795)
[796](https://docs.rs#796)Note that in verbose mode, whitespace is ignored everywhere, including within
[797](https://docs.rs#797)character classes. To insert whitespace, use its escaped form or a hex literal.
[798](https://docs.rs#798)For example, `\ ` or `\x20` for an ASCII space.
[799](https://docs.rs#799)
[800](https://docs.rs#800)Flags can be toggled within a pattern. Here's an example that matches
[801](https://docs.rs#801)case-insensitively for the first part but case-sensitively for the second part:
[802](https://docs.rs#802)
[803](https://docs.rs#803)```rust
[804](https://docs.rs#804)use regex::Regex;
[805](https://docs.rs#805)
[806](https://docs.rs#806)let re = Regex::new(r"(?i)a+(?-i)b+").unwrap();
[807](https://docs.rs#807)let m = re.find("AaAaAbbBBBb").unwrap();
[808](https://docs.rs#808)assert_eq!(m.as_str(), "AaAaAbb");
[809](https://docs.rs#809)```
[810](https://docs.rs#810)
[811](https://docs.rs#811)Notice that the `a+` matches either `a` or `A`, but the `b+` only matches
[812](https://docs.rs#812)`b`.
[813](https://docs.rs#813)
[814](https://docs.rs#814)Multi-line mode means `^` and `$` no longer match just at the beginning/end of
[815](https://docs.rs#815)the input, but also at the beginning/end of lines:
[816](https://docs.rs#816)
[817](https://docs.rs#817)```
[818](https://docs.rs#818)use regex::Regex;
[819](https://docs.rs#819)
[820](https://docs.rs#820)let re = Regex::new(r"(?m)^line \d+").unwrap();
[821](https://docs.rs#821)let m = re.find("line one\nline 2\n").unwrap();
[822](https://docs.rs#822)assert_eq!(m.as_str(), "line 2");
[823](https://docs.rs#823)```
[824](https://docs.rs#824)
[825](https://docs.rs#825)Note that `^` matches after new lines, even at the end of input:
[826](https://docs.rs#826)
[827](https://docs.rs#827)```
[828](https://docs.rs#828)use regex::Regex;
[829](https://docs.rs#829)
[830](https://docs.rs#830)let re = Regex::new(r"(?m)^").unwrap();
[831](https://docs.rs#831)let m = re.find_iter("test\n").last().unwrap();
[832](https://docs.rs#832)assert_eq!((m.start(), m.end()), (5, 5));
[833](https://docs.rs#833)```
[834](https://docs.rs#834)
[835](https://docs.rs#835)When both CRLF mode and multi-line mode are enabled, then `^` and `$` will
[836](https://docs.rs#836)match either `\r` or `\n`, but never in the middle of a `\r\n`:
[837](https://docs.rs#837)
[838](https://docs.rs#838)```
[839](https://docs.rs#839)use regex::Regex;
[840](https://docs.rs#840)
[841](https://docs.rs#841)let re = Regex::new(r"(?mR)^foo$").unwrap();
[842](https://docs.rs#842)let m = re.find("\r\nfoo\r\n").unwrap();
[843](https://docs.rs#843)assert_eq!(m.as_str(), "foo");
[844](https://docs.rs#844)```
[845](https://docs.rs#845)
[846](https://docs.rs#846)Unicode mode can also be selectively disabled, although only when the result
[847](https://docs.rs#847)*would not* match invalid UTF-8. One good example of this is using an ASCII
[848](https://docs.rs#848)word boundary instead of a Unicode word boundary, which might make some regex
[849](https://docs.rs#849)searches run faster:
[850](https://docs.rs#850)
[851](https://docs.rs#851)```rust
[852](https://docs.rs#852)use regex::Regex;
[853](https://docs.rs#853)
[854](https://docs.rs#854)let re = Regex::new(r"(?-u:\b).+(?-u:\b)").unwrap();
[855](https://docs.rs#855)let m = re.find("$$abc$$").unwrap();
[856](https://docs.rs#856)assert_eq!(m.as_str(), "abc");
[857](https://docs.rs#857)```
[858](https://docs.rs#858)
[859](https://docs.rs#859)### Escape sequences
[860](https://docs.rs#860)
[861](https://docs.rs#861)Note that this includes all possible escape sequences, even ones that are
[862](https://docs.rs#862)documented elsewhere.
[863](https://docs.rs#863)
[864](https://docs.rs#864)<pre class="rust">
[865](https://docs.rs#865)\*              literal *, applies to all ASCII except [0-9A-Za-z<>]
[866](https://docs.rs#866)\a              bell (\x07)
[867](https://docs.rs#867)\f              form feed (\x0C)
[868](https://docs.rs#868)\t              horizontal tab
[869](https://docs.rs#869)\n              new line
[870](https://docs.rs#870)\r              carriage return
[871](https://docs.rs#871)\v              vertical tab (\x0B)
[872](https://docs.rs#872)\A              matches at the beginning of a haystack
[873](https://docs.rs#873)\z              matches at the end of a haystack
[874](https://docs.rs#874)\b              word boundary assertion
[875](https://docs.rs#875)\B              negated word boundary assertion
[876](https://docs.rs#876)\b{start}, \<   start-of-word boundary assertion
[877](https://docs.rs#877)\b{end}, \>     end-of-word boundary assertion
[878](https://docs.rs#878)\b{start-half}  half of a start-of-word boundary assertion
[879](https://docs.rs#879)\b{end-half}    half of a end-of-word boundary assertion
[880](https://docs.rs#880)\123            octal character code, up to three digits (when enabled)
[881](https://docs.rs#881)\x7F            hex character code (exactly two digits)
[882](https://docs.rs#882)\x{10FFFF}      any hex character code corresponding to a Unicode code point
[883](https://docs.rs#883)\u007F          hex character code (exactly four digits)
[884](https://docs.rs#884)\u{7F}          any hex character code corresponding to a Unicode code point
[885](https://docs.rs#885)\U0000007F      hex character code (exactly eight digits)
[886](https://docs.rs#886)\U{7F}          any hex character code corresponding to a Unicode code point
[887](https://docs.rs#887)\p{Letter}      Unicode character class
[888](https://docs.rs#888)\P{Letter}      negated Unicode character class
[889](https://docs.rs#889)\d, \s, \w      Perl character class
[890](https://docs.rs#890)\D, \S, \W      negated Perl character class
[891](https://docs.rs#891)</pre>
